critical_observation_model_load_24_minut.what_happened: Model load phase began at 09:54:42 wall-clock. Next log line (Prefill patch applied) was at 10:18:53 — a 24-minute, 11-second gap. Python's internal timer reports 'Model loaded in 23.0s' which is 60x smaller than wall-clock.
critical_observation_model_load_24_minut.interpretation: The process was paged out during the model load. Python's timing measurement runs inside the Python interpreter's CPU budget, so when the OS suspends the process due to memory pressure, the Python timer stops ticking. The ~23s of active work took ~24 minutes of wall-clock to complete. Effective CPU-share was 23 / 1441 = 1.6%.
critical_observation_model_load_24_minut.implications_for_profiler: Task #8's profiler samples phys_footprint_gb and cpu_pct — but samples are taken from within the Python process, so when the process is paged out, NO samples are taken. The profiler is blind to wall-clock periods when the process gets zero CPU. This creates a profile-timing gap: profile.json shows 23s of activity but wall-clock shows 1441s. The `num_samples` count will be proportional to Python-active time, not wall-clock.
critical_observation_model_load_24_minut.filing_as_task: This is a real analyst observation but it's a profiler blind spot, not a hypercar-goal regression. Task #8 is already closed. Filing as a new task below (#77) to add wall-clock correlation to the profiler output so future runs can detect 'model loaded in 23s but wall was 24m' patterns automatically.
